newsitem.title: USA: Fruits, vegetables, dairy reduce blood pressure.
newsitem.headline: Fruits, vegetables, dairy reduce blood pressure.

text.p: Low-fat dairy products added to a diet rich in fruits and vegetables can reduce high blood pressure significantly and dramatically cut the risk of heart disease and stroke, a study in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine concluded.

The results, based on evaluations of 459 volunteers who ate widely available foods, suggest that a diet rich in those three food groups works better than a diet that emphasizes fruits and vegetables alone.

A team led by Dr. Lawrence Appel of Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore found the fruit-vegetable-dairy diet, as long as it was low in fat, lowered systolic blood pressure (the higher number on a reading) by 5.5 points and diastolic blood pressure (the lower number) by three points compared to a regular diet of standard U.S. fare.

The study also found that the fruits and vegetables diet lowered blood pressure by 2.8 points for the systolic reading and 1.1 point for the diastolic blood pressure reading compared to a regular diet.
Widespread adoption of the combination diet, the team said, could potentially reduce the risk of heart disease by 15 percent and the likelihood of stroke by 27 percent.

The diet consisted of five daily servings of fruits and juices, four servings of vegetables, two servings of low-fat dairy products, less than one serving of snacks or sweets and two to three servings of fats, oils and salad dressing. There was one serving of beef, pork or ham every other day.

The "fruits and vegetables" diet was similar, except for the exclusion of dairy products and inclusion of two servings of meat daily and twice as much fats, oils or salad dressing as the dairy diet. People eating the regular American diet got only two daily servings of fruits and vegetables each.

Doctors have known for years that diet can influence blood pressure. Advice to reduce weight, use less salt and drink less alcohol has been based on diet studies. Vegetarians also tend to have lower blood pressures than meat eaters.
Researchers have tried to lower blood pressure by giving volunteers specific nutrients but those efforts have not produced dramatic results.
The new test used volunteers who ate standardized meals for 11 weeks. The diets were designed to prevent anyone from gaining or losing weight, which can influence blood pressure.

After three weeks of a "control" diet low in fruits, vegetables and dairy products, the volunteers were split into three groups. About a third continued on the control diet, a third got the fruits and vegetables diet and the rest got the low-fat, fruit-vegetable-dairy diet.

Blood pressures for those who ate the fruits and vegetables and low-fat fruit-vegetable-dairy diets dropped after two weeks and the readings stayed down for the next six weeks. The diet works for both men and women of all races.
"By using commonly available foods, including meats, the trial tested dietary patterns that the general U.S. population potentially could adopt," the Appel team concluded.
The study was not designed "to identify the effective and ineffective components of the diets," they said.
